title: Rocky Sucks

jokes.text: The President interrupts a national emergency briefing to take a call about covering a baby seal birth at the zoo
jokes.setup: The President is describing a grave national crisis and calls on Dwayne Johnson for help in a moment of solemn urgency
jokes.punchline: The dramatic meeting is immediately deflated by a phone notification about covering a baby seal birth — the most trivial possible contrast
jokes.explanation: Classic bathos — high stakes punctured by the utterly mundane. The baby seal specificity is good, and the timing of interrupting a 'national emergency' is clean. Not extraordinary but well-executed cold open work.

jokes.text: Dwayne throws the key away with prompting — a brief physical beat suggesting they're locking someone out or disposing of something awkwardly
jokes.setup: Someone asks if Dwayne is going to throw a key away
jokes.punchline: He does it — the wordless completion of an absurd action, presumably locking someone out ceremonially
jokes.explanation: Context is too opaque in transcript form. The beat exists and is presumably visual, but without knowing who/what the key is for, it lands as a mild gag at best. Scored low because context doesn't support full comedic impact from transcript alone.

jokes.text: The country of 'Gjelgjiughm' — a clearly unpronounceable nonsense country name delivered with straight-faced gravitas
jokes.setup: The President is explaining a serious geopolitical coffee crisis and introduces a key foreign nation
jokes.punchline: The nation's name is 'Gjelgjiughm' — an almost comically unpronounceable string of consonants delivered as if it were perfectly normal
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the word itself — pure absurdist name comedy. The economy is excellent: no explanation needed, the name does all the work. The deadpan delivery implied by the setup elevates it. Rewatch bonus because you notice it anew each time you hear someone try to say it.

jokes.text: Dwayne responds to 'Are you familiar with Gjelgjiughm?' with: 'Took home gold, silver, and bronze in skeet shooting during the 2028 Olympics.' / '...No.' / 'Then no.'
jokes.setup: The President asks if Dwayne knows this tiny, insular, unremarkable country — implying the answer is obviously no
jokes.punchline: Dwayne has a weirdly hyper-specific piece of knowledge about them (future Olympics skeet shooting sweep), which is immediately negated when the President says 'No,' causing Dwayne to also say 'Then no' — disowning his own answer
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional. Three layers of comedy: (1) the absurdly specific knowledge about a fictional obscure nation, (2) the future tense '2028 Olympics' implying a Dwayne-in-the-future world, (3) the perfect structural pivot of 'Then no' — Dwayne immediately abandoning his own position. The economy is flawless. The character integration is high — only someone with Dwayne's cultural omnivore energy would have this weird niche knowledge. This approaches the 8.0 anchor quality comfortably and exceeds it.

jokes.text: 'You throw one bean in the air, two come back in your face.'
jokes.setup: The President is explaining that Gjelgjiughm has an abundance of coffee beans
jokes.punchline: The folksy metaphor used to describe the abundance is surreally specific and physically nonsensical — beans don't come back in your face
jokes.explanation: A pleasantly strange image delivered as if it were a normal idiom. The specific detail of 'two come back in your face' is the right kind of weird — it implies slapstick physics while just describing agricultural abundance. Good economy.

jokes.text: The hot mic incident: Prime Minister Honig says the President's 'hands are soft as marshmallows, pillowy as a duchess' — then the President defensively adds 'My hands are out of frame on purpose. My hands are my best feature.'
jokes.setup: The President explains the PM rejected his trade deal because she hates him, revealed via a hot mic moment where she insults him
jokes.punchline: The insult lands on his soft hands — and rather than deny it, the President doubles down that his hands are his BEST feature, which is both a non-denial and a self-own
jokes.explanation: 'Soft as marshmallows, pillowy as a duchess' is strong insult writing — specific, vivid, slightly archaic. The President's response reveals his vanity while accidentally confirming the insult. 'Pillowy as a duchess' is particularly good wordplay.

jokes.text: Dwayne asks if there's a wrestler code for a real injury, and the answer is just: 'Ugh, my knee. Augh, I hurt my knee.'
jokes.setup: Wrestlers use elaborate kayfabe to protect the fiction of the sport; one would expect a clever or elaborate secret code
jokes.punchline: The 'code' is just… saying you hurt your knee, with no code at all — the deflation of expectation is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic anti-climactic reveal. The setup creates genuine curiosity — wrestling kayfabe is rich territory — and the payoff subverts it completely. Maximum economy: the non-code is stated twice, as if showing you how basic it really is.

jokes.text: 'You put your body on the line, it's good to know they appreciate it.' — delivered while the crowd chants 'Rocky sucks!'
jokes.setup: Rocky has just described the fans chanting 'Rocky sucks' while he performed
jokes.punchline: Bruno responds with apparent sincerity about fan appreciation — pure sarcasm delivered deadpan against the evidence
jokes.explanation: Functional irony that works because of the visual/audio contrast (fans chanting 'Rocky sucks' while Bruno expresses appreciation). Not a sophisticated joke but clean and serviceable.

jokes.text: Dwayne says the origin of 'add insult to injury' is probably from this exact situation — crowd chanting 'Rocky sucks' while he's injured
jokes.setup: Rocky is literally injured (knee) while simultaneously being insulted by the crowd
jokes.punchline: He muses that this situation — injury + insult — is probably where the idiom 'add insult to injury' comes from, with Bruno's dry 'Yeah, probably, Bruno. Probably.'
jokes.explanation: A pleasantly self-aware meta-linguistic joke — the character literally embodying the idiom and noticing it. Bruno's response of 'Yeah, probably, Bruno. Probably' (talking to himself) adds a nice layer of absurdity.

jokes.text: While trying to smile and endure the 'Rocky sucks' chants, Rocky's knee buckles — but it turns out a popcorn kernel fell in his boot
jokes.setup: Rocky says he'll 'smile and take it' stoically — implying we'll see composure under fire
jokes.punchline: He immediately winces, setting up a knee injury fake-out, but it's just a popcorn kernel — the mundane deflates the dramatic
jokes.explanation: Nice two-beat misdirect: first we think knee injury recurrence, then the popcorn kernel deflates it. Bruno's response — 'Lord ain't grantin' you no dignity today' — is the actual punchline and elevates this above the physical gag alone.

jokes.text: 'Lord ain't grantin' you no dignity today.'
jokes.setup: Rocky is being chanted against AND has a popcorn kernel in his boot while trying to maintain dignity
jokes.punchline: Bruno's philosophical resignation — the universe has specifically withdrawn dignity from Rocky today — delivered with perfect comic timing
jokes.explanation: This is a standout line. 'Lord ain't grantin' you no dignity today' is specific, character-true (Bruno's voice is distinct and earthy), maximally economical, and quotable. The double negative gives it a folk-wisdom cadence that makes it feel real. This reaches the 8.0 anchor: it has the precision and character specificity of a great sitcom line.

jokes.text: Rocky's father says 'That's terrible news, son' about the no-surgery diagnosis — which is actually good news
jokes.setup: The doctor says no surgery needed — objectively good news for an athlete
jokes.punchline: Father responds 'That's terrible news, son' — seemingly misunderstanding, which is then corrected by another character
jokes.explanation: Mild confusion/misunderstanding gag. Works slightly because of the character's bluntness being played against the actual good news, but it's a well-worn structure.

jokes.text: Father: 'Babe, don't sugarcoat it. When a wrestler isn't over with the fans, which you are not...' / Rocky: 'Yes, I know. Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Father is ostensibly trying to help Rocky understand his situation, but delivers brutal honesty with no softening
jokes.punchline: Rocky's exasperated 'Yes, I know. Thank you.' — the 'thank you' being sarcastic acknowledgment that dad has helpfully piled on
jokes.explanation: Good cringe family dynamic — the father's bluntness being the source of discomfort while Rocky has to maintain composure. The rhythm of interruption and Rocky's weary response is well-executed.

jokes.text: Mother: 'He is delicate.' / Rocky: 'I'm not delicate.' / Mother: 'I say you are delicate; You are delicate, Dewey.'
jokes.setup: Rocky tries to assert his toughness amid family babying him
jokes.punchline: Mother overrides his protest with pure maternal authority — 'I say you are delicate; you are delicate' — the logic being circular and absolute
jokes.explanation: The comedy of maternal absolute authority overriding a 6'5" professional wrestler's self-image is rich. 'I say you are delicate; You are delicate, Dewey' — the use of his childhood name seals it. Great character integration: the visual comedy of this huge man being called 'delicate' by his mother is implicit and perfect.

jokes.text: Dany doesn't believe in throw pillows — 'She says they just take up space.' / 'They just take up... what?'
jokes.setup: Rocky is injured in bed and needs more pillows; mother offers to get them, noting Dany's anti-throw-pillow philosophy
jokes.punchline: The incredulous 'They just take up... WHAT?' from Rocky's side — the sheer incomprehensibility of someone opposing throw pillows treated as a major character flaw
jokes.explanation: Funny domestic detail — the anti-throw-pillow stance as a character reveal for Dany, and the family's scandalized reaction to it. The reaction beat of 'what?' is well-placed.

jokes.text: 'Popped pecks pay rent checks.'
jokes.setup: Rocky is showing gym merchandise designs and father is advising on which neckline to go with for the T-shirts
jokes.punchline: Father delivers this alliterative folk-wisdom maxim with complete conviction — it rhymes, it's absurd as business advice, but it has an internal logic
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional. 'Popped pecks pay rent checks' works on multiple levels: the alliteration gives it a self-contained rhythmic satisfaction, it's absurd as genuine business wisdom yet somehow true in the wrestling world, and it's completely character-specific to a wrestling patriarch with old-school showman sensibility. The economy is near-perfect — five words that tell you everything about the character and get a big laugh. This comfortably reaches 8+ territory.

jokes.text: 'She's supposed to be a silent partner.' / 'You said that, not me.'
jokes.setup: Dany has been actively opining on Rocky's gym merchandise despite being the financial backer
jokes.punchline: Rocky tries to invoke her 'silent partner' status to dismiss her input; Dany immediately signals she never agreed to that framing
jokes.explanation: Quick, functional domestic comedy exchange. The beat lands but isn't especially original — the 'you said it, I didn't' dynamic is familiar. Clean execution saves it.

jokes.text: 'Have everything in writing.' / 'We don't need that. We are family.' / 'I'm gonna stay out of it. But-but...'
jokes.setup: Mother gives sensible business advice to put their gym partnership in writing
jokes.punchline: Dany refuses because 'we are family' — and then Rocky's awkward 'I'm gonna stay out of it. But-but...' signals he knows trouble is brewing but is caught between wife and mother
jokes.explanation: The cringe of watching Rocky try to stay neutral in an obvious future conflict is funny, especially the 'But-but...' trailing off. Functional situational comedy.

jokes.text: Rocky's complaint about rehab: 'My only complaint is my physical therapist keeps referring to it as "our knee."'
jokes.setup: Rocky is reporting on his successful rehab — things are going well
jokes.punchline: The only complaint is a minor but very relatable annoyance — a PT's over-possessive language about the patient's body part
jokes.explanation: Strong observational joke — the physical therapist saying 'our knee' is a real phenomenon and the specificity makes it land. It captures a genuine but rarely-articulated social awkwardness with perfect economy. Particularly funny coming from someone as large and ownership-focused as Dwayne.

jokes.text: WWF executive gives completely vague non-answer about when Rocky returns: 'When we make a decision, we'll give you a call.' / Rocky: 'Cool. Cool. So, like, uh, when?'
jokes.setup: Rocky asks directly when he'll be brought back; the exec gives a corporate non-answer
jokes.punchline: Rocky immediately re-asks the same question as if the non-answer hadn't just happened — the comic persistence of asking 'when' after being explicitly told 'when we decide'
jokes.explanation: The comic deflation of corporate speak followed by Rocky's oblivious re-ask is a well-worn structure but executed cleanly. The 'Cool. Cool.' before re-asking is a nice character beat.

jokes.text: Criminology minor from Miami cutaway: Rocky contemplates his options, his criminology minor is mentioned, then immediate cut to: 'Detective Johnson, here's the victim.' / 'Oh, God. Another child.' / 'Actually, sir, victim was full-grown adult male.' / pause / 'You're just really big.'
jokes.setup: Dany suggests Rocky has options if wrestling doesn't work — specifically his criminology minor from Miami. This leads to an imagined cutaway of Rocky as a detective.
jokes.punchline: The scene immediately plays out: Rocky is so enormous that a full-grown adult appears to be a child when he's standing next to him. The officer has to clarify the victim is an adult — 'You're just really big.'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. It's built on an extremely specific, character-integrated premise — only Dwayne Johnson's actual extraordinary physique makes this joke work. The structure is immaculate: setup (criminology minor), immediate cutaway visualization, misdirect ('Another child'), then the devastating correction ('You're just really big'). The implication that every crime scene looks like a child's death to Rocky is simultaneously dark and absurd. It reaches the 8+ threshold easily: it's comparable in quality to the Snip/snap anchor — character-specific, escalating, and quotable.

jokes.text: 'If wrestling doesn't work out, you'll always have that criminology minor from Miami.'
jokes.setup: Dany is encouraging Rocky by saying he has options beyond wrestling.
jokes.punchline: The 'option' is a criminology minor — not even a major, not a career, a minor — as a fallback for a professional wrestler. The cutaway to a detective scene immediately follows.
jokes.explanation: The setup works because the 'options' framing primes you for something substantial. A criminology minor as a backup plan is funny on its own, but it works double duty as a setup for the detective cutaway that follows. Good structural payoff.

jokes.text: 'She ain't pregnant, is she?' at the wedding
jokes.setup: Father expresses happiness at the wedding
jokes.punchline: Immediately undercuts it with the blunt inquiry about whether Dany is pregnant — implying that's the only reason for an unexpected wedding
jokes.explanation: Standard blunt-father joke, elevated slightly by the follow-up: 'Cause she's drinkin' a lot for a pregnant woman.' The observation is its own comedic beat — the father has been watching and assessing. Serviceable.

jokes.text: 'Cause she drinkin' a lot for a pregnant woman.'
jokes.setup: Rocky denies Dany is pregnant
jokes.punchline: Father has apparently been monitoring Dany's alcohol consumption as evidence and delivers the observation as logical reasoning — the specificity of his surveillance is funnier than the joke itself
jokes.explanation: The follow-up beats the original setup. The father's casual, observational monitoring of Dany's drinking as pregnancy evidence reveals a specific, funny character logic. 'A lot for a pregnant woman' implies he has a calibrated threshold for acceptable pregnant-woman drinking, which is its own absurdity.

jokes.text: The wedding gift: a microwave that's also a radio — with presets of 'defrost, popcorn, and Cool 101.5'
jokes.setup: They're opening wedding gifts; this one is unusual
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'Cool 101.5' as a radio preset on a microwave/radio combo is perfectly absurd — someone programmed a smooth jazz station into a kitchen appliance
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist product comedy. The escalation from 'defrost' and 'popcorn' (functional) to 'Cool 101.5' (a specific radio station) is perfectly structured — you expect one more microwave function and get an AM/FM station instead. The gift also becomes a running thread through the episode (Vince sent it, it's recalled, gets replaced by a blender).

jokes.text: 'Maybe keep it under your kitchen sink.'
jokes.setup: The microwave-radio gift has been revealed as bizarre
jokes.punchline: Mother's pragmatic solution is to hide it under the sink — the dismissive practicality of the suggestion acknowledges how terrible the gift is
jokes.explanation: Efficient follow-up beat. The specificity of 'under the sink' as the disposal location for an unwanted wedding gift is good — it's not the trash, which would be rude, but it's just as dismissive. Quick and clean.

jokes.text: The microwave-radio is from Vince — who RSVP'd yes to the wedding but didn't show up
jokes.setup: The bizarre microwave-radio gift is traced to Vince, who also stood up the wedding
jokes.punchline: Vince sent the most passive-aggressive, negligent possible wedding gift AND didn't attend — the combination reveals his character perfectly
jokes.explanation: The joke works retroactively — now the bizarre gift makes sense as a Vince power move. It recontextualizes the absurdist gift as character-specific behavior. Rewatch bonus because the gift's absurdity gains new meaning.

jokes.text: Wedding guest who is disappointed about the absence of roasted pig: 'Look, I'm not gonna say I'm disappointed, but, uh, I was really expecting a roasted pig for this occasion.'
jokes.setup: A guest is asked to say a few words about the couple on their big day
jokes.punchline: He immediately redirects to his disappointment about the pig — leading with 'I'm not gonna say I'm disappointed' before saying he's disappointed
jokes.explanation: The self-contradiction ('I'm not gonna say I'm disappointed' / immediately says he's disappointed) plus the laser focus on the pig over the couple is a clean character gag. Works as a running thread setup too.

jokes.text: Macho Man Randy Savage interrupts a financial conversation about Dany's work at Merrill Lynch: 'I believe in an unbalanced portfolio. Yeah. Risk and aggression... Now that is what the Macho Man is all about, baby. Yeah, dig it.'
jokes.setup: A guest is talking about Dany's work at Merrill Lynch — a normal wedding conversation
jokes.punchline: Macho Man interrupts with his signature aggressive persona applied to financial advice — the collision of 'Macho Man' wrestling character energy with investment portfolio theory
jokes.explanation: The Macho Man applying his persona to financial advice is a perfect character joke. 'I believe in an unbalanced portfolio. Risk and aggression.' actually has its own deranged internal logic as investment philosophy — and then 'that is what the Macho Man is all about, baby' collapses the character back into wrestling mode. The 'Yeah, dig it' capper is pure Savage. High character integration score: this could ONLY be this character.

jokes.text: Macho Man: 'Sorry, I think I'm drinking out of your glass. Can't keep it straight.'
jokes.setup: Macho Man has been in character the whole scene
jokes.punchline: He snaps to completely normal, self-aware social awkwardness — apologizing for the glass mix-up like a regular person — the tonal whiplash from his unhinged persona to mundane politeness
jokes.explanation: Excellent deflation of the Macho Man persona. The tonal whiplash from bombastic wrestling character to 'sorry I think I'm drinking out of your glass' is perfectly executed. The comedy comes from treating Randy Savage as a real person at a party who has normal social moments. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: Pig-obsessed guest's extended lament: 'I purposely didn't eat pig yesterday 'cause I thought for sure that we were gonna have pig today... And there-there-there's no pig.'
jokes.setup: The guest already expressed pig disappointment; now he elaborates with the full scale of his sacrifice and planning
jokes.punchline: He reveals he strategically abstained from pig the day before specifically to enjoy it today — the planning, the sacrifice, the hope — and now there's no pig. The trailing 'And there-there-there's no pig' is a comedic landing.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of pig grief is excellent. 'I purposely didn't eat pig yesterday' is the setup that reveals the depth of his commitment, and 'there-there-there's no pig' is the defeated, stutter-punctuated conclusion. The stutter on 'there' is key — it's not just the absence of pig, it's the inability to process it. Great running gag payoff.

jokes.text: Salt-N-Pepa's 'Push It' plays at the wedding; guests speculate: 'So how long do we think until one of these guys splits their pants?' / 'That's why ol' Bruno always travels with a sewing kit.'
jokes.setup: Professional wrestlers dancing at a wedding to Salt-N-Pepa
jokes.punchline: The practical concern about pants durability given the physiques involved — and Bruno's preparedness with a sewing kit confirms this is a recurring concern in wrestling social situations
jokes.explanation: Good character-world specific observational comedy — the practical problem of wrestlers in formal wear dancing is a real and funny concern. Bruno's sewing kit preparedness being routine implies a whole history of wrestling wardrobe malfunctions.

jokes.text: 'Vince doesn't send a gold-plated microwave that's also a radio to wrestlers he doesn't believe in.' / 'Oh, that's what you always say, huh?'
jokes.setup: Bruno is trying to reassure that Vince's bizarre gift signals faith in Rocky
jokes.punchline: Bruno delivers this as a well-worn life maxim — 'that's what you always say' — implying he has repeated this specific piece of wisdom about microwave-radios before, which is absurd since the gift is one-of-a-kind
jokes.explanation: This is a standout comedic moment. The callback to the microwave-radio is used to construct a fake folk-wisdom saying, and then 'that's what you always say, huh?' implies Bruno has a whole repertoire of microwave-radio proverbs. It's meta-absurdist: a nonsensical specific saying being treated as a time-tested wisdom. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor example in structure and quotability.

jokes.text: 'That boy's got 10,000 lives. And I don't think we've even seen three of them yet.'
jokes.setup: Guest is commenting on Rocky's resilience and future potential
jokes.punchline: The '10,000 lives' is absurdist hyperbole for resilience, but then the qualifier 'I don't think we've even seen three of them yet' is the comedic payoff — establishing a universe in which this is a measurable, trackable fact
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it doesn't stop at the hyperbole — it extends the metaphor logically, implying there are countable remaining lives. Given that this is The Rock with a well-known massive career trajectory, 'we haven't even seen three' is extra resonant. The rewatch bonus is high because of dramatic irony.

jokes.text: 'Oh, that's what you always say, huh?' — Ata's dry response to Bruno's fake aphorism.
jokes.setup: Bruno presents the microwave-radio aphorism as something he 'always says.'
jokes.punchline: Ata's single deadpan line calls out the absurdity without belaboring it — the skeptical 'that's what you always say, huh' implies she knows this isn't a real saying.
jokes.explanation: The perfect straight-man button on joke #34. Maximum economy — 8 words that land perfectly as punctuation. Raises the craft of the preceding joke by catching its absurdity with exactly the right tone.

jokes.text: 'Come to think of it, I owe the kid a headband.'
jokes.setup: The speaker has been warmly reminiscing about knowing Rocky since he was young
jokes.punchline: The sudden pivot to a specific, petty debt — a headband — undercuts the sentiment completely and with perfect non sequitur energy
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical non sequitur. After warm sentiment, the hard pivot to 'I owe the kid a headband' is both funny and character-specific to wrestling culture (where headbands are actual equipment). The specificity of 'a headband' over any other item is key — it's small enough to be funny but wrestling-specific enough to feel real.

jokes.text: Hulk Hogan arrives and Rocky says he forgot to mention 'black tie' didn't mean 'black mustache'
jokes.setup: Hogan arrives at the 'black tie' wedding
jokes.punchline: Rocky gently notes the black tie dress code did not extend to a bleached-blonde/black mustache look
jokes.explanation: The joke requires knowing Hogan's iconic appearance — bleach-blonde hair with black mustache — which makes the 'black tie / black mustache' wordplay land perfectly. High character integration: this joke is entirely dependent on Hogan's specific, immediately recognizable look.

jokes.text: Hogan: 'The bleach job is hell on my nostrils.' / Rocky: 'It's hell on my eyes, too.'
jokes.setup: The black mustache/bleach joke has been established
jokes.punchline: Hogan admits the bleach affects him too (nostrils), and Rocky agrees it affects his eyes — both men acknowledging the look is problematic, but Hogan is still doing it
jokes.explanation: Hogan's self-awareness about his own look's sensory impact is funny. The exchange works as a mutual acknowledgment that the look is objectively problematic while clearly indicating neither man is going to do anything about it. Clean follow-up beat.

jokes.text: Hogan on Rocky Maivia's persona: 'You've got more personality than what you're showing.' / 'He's so...' / 'Earnest?' / 'I was gonna say punchable.'
jokes.setup: Hogan is complimenting Rocky, searching for the right word to describe his current bland persona
jokes.punchline: Rocky offers 'earnest' as a flattering interpretation; Hogan corrects it to 'punchable' — the brutal honesty of 'punchable' as the accurate descriptor, and then graciously accepting 'earnest' as a secondary synonym
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: Rocky offers the charitable reading, Hogan gives the true one ('punchable'), and then graciously allows 'earnest is good too' as a retroactive synonym. The word 'punchable' as a wrestling critique is doubly resonant — in wrestling, you literally get punched — and as a character description it's viciously accurate and specific. This clearly exceeds the 8.0 anchor in structure and quotability.

jokes.text: Hogan's stomach can't handle dairy at the wedding; 'I'll hit the dance floor and blame Macho.'
jokes.setup: Hogan asks for lactase (for dairy intolerance) but can't get it
jokes.punchline: He decides to drink the dairy anyway and pre-assigns blame for whatever happens to Macho Man — the preemptive scapegoating
jokes.explanation: The logic of 'I'll do the thing that will make me gassy and preemptively blame Macho Man on the dance floor' is wonderfully specific. It implies a social dynamic between Hogan and Savage where this kind of blame-shifting is normal. 'I'll hit the dance floor and blame Macho' is quotable as a general life strategy.

jokes.text: Vince calls to congratulate on the wedding and says: 'Don't use it [the microwave]. It's been recalled. Cancer stuff. Terrible product. I'm sending you a blender instead.'
jokes.setup: Rocky thanks Vince for the microwave-radio gift
jokes.punchline: Vince reveals it's been recalled for cancer — treats this as minor news ('terrible product'), and offhandedly promises a replacement blender as if this resolves everything
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff. The microwave-radio's absurdity is now explained: it was a defective, cancer-causing recalled product. Vince's casual 'Cancer stuff. Terrible product.' is darkly perfect — he treats it like a minor inconvenience and immediately pivots to the blender replacement as if that's fully adequate. The character work is sharp: Vince is oblivious to gift-giving etiquette and treats a cancer recall as mildly embarrassing rather than alarming.

jokes.text: 'That's so weird. Biloxi was my second choice for honeymoon destinations.'
jokes.setup: Vince tells Rocky to come back to wrestling in Biloxi in a week — right after his wedding
jokes.punchline: Rocky's response that Biloxi was his second honeymoon choice is (a) absurd as a honeymoon destination and (b) a perfect anti-complain — framing the inconvenience as cosmically convenient
jokes.explanation: Biloxi, Mississippi as a second-choice honeymoon destination is inherently funny — it's a specific downgrade from anywhere tropical. Rocky's cheerful framing of it as coincidence rather than imposition reveals character. Good economy.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, I was a big Hart Foundation fan. I like a guy with the confidence to wear pink pants.'
jokes.setup: Discussion of WWF factions and crew gimmicks
jokes.punchline: Rocky's endorsement of the Hart Foundation is specifically tied to the confidence required to wear pink pants — reducing the team's entire appeal to a fashion statement
jokes.explanation: Bret Hart's pink ring gear was genuinely iconic. Rocky reframing the entire Hart Foundation legacy through the lens of 'confidence to wear pink pants' is a funny deflation that also genuinely captures something true about that wrestling aesthetic.

jokes.text: Rocky joins the Nation wearing denim shorts — 'Booyah!' / 'Wait, that was your bad dude look? Are those denim shorts?'
jokes.setup: Dwayne describes his dramatic 'heel turn' as becoming 'one bad dude'
jokes.punchline: The 'bad dude' debut involves denim shorts — the interviewer's incredulous 'Are those denim shorts?' punctures the grandiosity
jokes.explanation: The gap between Rocky's self-image ('one bad dude') and the visual reality ('denim shorts') is a strong image-based joke. The 'Booyah!' followed by the denim shorts reveal is a classic subverted expectation. Rocky's defense — 'that was the fashion of the time' — adds a third beat.

jokes.text: 'Be honest. I get a pop at all out there? It felt quiet.' / 'I'ma always shoot you straight. You ain't pop worth a damn.' / 'Straight out the gate, huh?' / 'Snap, crackle, no pop.' / 'And you're still going.' / 'Orville Redenbacher you are not.'
jokes.setup: Rocky asks if he got a crowd reaction (a 'pop') after joining the Nation
jokes.punchline: Farooq says no pop, then extends the cereal/popcorn metaphor: 'Snap, crackle, no pop' → 'Orville Redenbacher you are not' — escalating the pop/popcorn wordplay through brand name
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's crown jewel. The structure is exceptional: 'pop' (wrestling term for crowd reaction) → 'snap, crackle, no pop' (Rice Krispies minus the pop) → Rocky protests the escalation ('and you're still going') → 'Orville Redenbacher you are not' (popcorn brand, completing the food escalation while also being a devastating character assessment). Three distinct wordplay moves in rapid succession, each funnier than the last. The Rocky protest 'and you're still going' is a structural masterstroke — it makes Farooq's commitment to the bit funnier. This clears the 9.5 anchor threshold in craft; it's comparable to the 'Snip, snap, snip, snap' example in structure, escalation, and quotability.

jokes.text: 'Hey, uh, be honest. I get a pop at all out there? It felt quiet.' / 'I'ma always shoot you straight. You ain't pop worth a damn.'
jokes.setup: Rocky just made his heel turn and joined the Nation, asking for honest feedback on the crowd reaction.
jokes.punchline: Farooq's 'you ain't pop worth a damn' — extremely direct — confirms what Rocky feared while being funnier than a softer answer.
jokes.explanation: A great straight-talk exchange. Farooq's economy ('you ain't pop worth a damn') is excellent — the wrestling-specific jargon ('pop') used as the metric makes it funnier and more specific. 'I'ma always shoot you straight' sets up the bluntness perfectly.

jokes.text: 'You're the fourth man in a four-man crew. I don't think Vince is thinking about your angles.'
jokes.setup: Rocky asks why Vince put him in the Nation and what his angle is
jokes.punchline: Farooq's blunt assessment: you're filler, he hasn't thought about you that deeply
jokes.explanation: Farooq's brutal directness as a character voice is established here and pays off in the pop/popcorn sequence. 'Fourth man in a four-man crew' is a perfect distillation of Rocky's invisibility problem. Good economy.

jokes.text: Pat interrupts the creative meeting by reading his time card: 'I worked one hour on Monday. Two hours on Tuesday. Wednesday was a bank holiday. Four hours on...' / 'Pat, you think I could get a few minutes with the boss?'
jokes.setup: Rocky is having an urgent creative conversation with Vince about mic time
jokes.punchline: Pat barges in to itemize his hours in excruciating, unhurried detail — oblivious to the importance of the conversation. 'Wednesday was a bank holiday' as if this is relevant information is particularly deadpan.
jokes.explanation: 'Wednesday was a bank holiday' as an inserted detail in a time card recitation to the boss is a nice touch of mundane bureaucracy invading a dramatic moment. The character of Pat as oblivious administrator works well.

jokes.text: Rocky negotiates mic time: 'If you gave me, like, 12 minutes...' / '2.' / 'I'll take it.' / '...2 1/2 would give me some time to work in some back story...' / '2 is fine.'
jokes.setup: Rocky has already agreed to 2 minutes of mic time
jokes.punchline: Having accepted 2, Rocky immediately tries to re-negotiate to 2.5 — and then catches himself and retreats to 2. The comedy is in the speed of his self-betrayal.
jokes.explanation: The negotiation beat is charming — Rocky folds immediately on the 12 minutes, takes 2, then almost immediately tries to add 30 seconds. The '2 is fine' correction from Vince completing the circuit is clean. Good rhythm.

jokes.text: Rocky's mother at the Raw broadcast: 'Rocky, pull up your tank. Your son's wife can see your chi-chis.' / Rocky Sr.: 'Everybody can see 'em.' / Rocky: 'I worked hard on these babies. Ba-boom!'
jokes.setup: Rocky is at the Raw broadcast about to deliver his career-defining promo
jokes.punchline: His mother's concern is not about the promo but about his chest being visible; father notes it's visible to everyone; Rocky is delighted by this and triumphant about his physique
jokes.explanation: 'Chi-chis' is a perfect word choice — maternal and slightly absurd for a massive wrestler's chest. The escalation from mother's concern → father's confirmation → Rocky's pride ('I worked hard on these babies. Ba-boom!') is a three-beat family comedy sequence. 'Ba-boom' as a self-celebration is a great character moment. Callbacks to the T-shirt/pecs theme.

jokes.text: 'Rocky Maivia's a lot of things, but sucks isn't one of them.'
jokes.setup: Rocky is delivering his heel promo and has recounted the 'Rocky sucks' chants
jokes.punchline: His rebuttal is the world's most minimal denial — he doesn't claim to be great, just not to suck — which is a perfectly calibrated piece of aggressive modesty
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional in its economy. He doesn't claim greatness — just not-suck. The understatement in the context of a heel promo (where you're supposed to brag) is perfectly calibrated. 'A lot of things, but sucks isn't one of them' has a beautiful rhythm and is a direct callback to the episode's title/theme. This is a 8+ moment: comparable to the anchor examples in quotability and economy.

jokes.text: Rocky's heel promo closer: 'Rocky Maivia and the new Nation of Domination lives, breathes, and dies respect.' delivered as villain speech — which is not how villainy usually works
jokes.setup: Rocky is delivering a heel/villain promo about how badass he is
jokes.punchline: His stated value is 'respect' — which is the most earnest, positive possible value for a villain to espouse. The contradiction between heel persona and the sentiment of 'we die for respect' is both funny and genuinely moving.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is subtle here — it's less a joke and more an irony. The 'villain' whose core motivation is respect is inherently sympathetic and somewhat absurd as villainy. Functions more as character drama than pure comedy, but there's a comedic irony worth noting.

jokes.text: 'Kind of like when I played Kim Jong Un, except no one saw it.' / 'I saw it.' / 'Yeah?' / 'Yeah. You were great.' / 'Thanks.' / 'You're welcome.'
jokes.setup: Rocky is comparing the feeling of his heel promo to expressing his authentic self in acting
jokes.punchline: He references playing Kim Jong Un (a real project that was abandoned/unseen), and the interviewer's 'I saw it' / 'You were great' / 'You're welcome' exchange is a perfect mini-comedy of polite support for obscure work
jokes.explanation: The reference to Dwayne Johnson actually being attached to a Kim Jong Un project is meta-real, and 'except no one saw it' is the self-deprecating acknowledgment of a real career footnote. The exchange that follows — 'I saw it' / 'Yeah? You were great' / 'Thanks' / 'You're welcome' — is a perfect miniature of polite hollow affirmation. The 'You're welcome' completing the loop without providing any useful information is especially good. High character integration: this only works because it references The Rock's real career.

jokes.text: Pat's feedback: 'You were more interesting in the last two minutes than you've been in the last six months.' / Rocky: 'Wow, okay. Everybody just out the gate with the honesty.'
jokes.setup: Rocky asks Pat for feedback after his promo
jokes.punchline: Pat's 'compliment' is structured as a devastating comparison — the subtext being that six months of work was less interesting than two minutes. Rocky's exasperated 'everybody just out the gate with the honesty' acknowledges the pattern of brutal feedback he's been receiving
jokes.explanation: Rocky's meta-commentary on the episode's running theme of brutally honest feedback is good. 'Everybody just out the gate with the honesty' is a callback to the pattern established by his father, Farooq, and now Pat. The observation works as both a joke and a running thread acknowledgment.

jokes.text: Pat's cat metaphor: 'Interesting isn't always necessarily good. You know? My cat throws up a human thumb. Is it interesting? Sure. But is it good? No.'
jokes.setup: Pat is qualifying his 'interesting' compliment to Rocky
jokes.punchline: The example chosen to illustrate the interesting-vs-good distinction is a cat vomiting a human thumb — a comically extreme and specific image that raises far more questions than it answers
jokes.explanation: Exceptional absurdist joke. The interesting/good distinction is real and worth making — Pat is a mentor figure offering genuine feedback — but the example of a cat vomiting a human thumb is so deranged it hijacks the entire conversation. The 'human thumb' specificity (not just a thumb, not just a finger, specifically human) takes a strange image and makes it stranger. Rocky's 'Did that really happen?' and Pat's 'Hey, stay focused' — dismissing the question — is perfect. This approaches the 9.0+ range in craft: genuinely unexpected, wildly specific, structurally sound.

jokes.text: Rocky: 'Did that really happen?' / Pat: 'Hey, stay focused.'
jokes.setup: Pat has just described his cat vomiting a human thumb
jokes.punchline: Rocky's natural reaction (did that really happen?) is stonewalled by Pat redirecting — the human thumb mystery is treated as irrelevant to the conversation at hand
jokes.explanation: The follow-up beat is essential to Joke 53's full impact. 'Stay focused' refuses to address whether the thumb incident was real — which makes it funnier by leaving it unresolved. The economy of 'Hey, stay focused' doing so much work earns the high economy score.

jokes.text: Prime Minister Honig has seen all of Dwayne's movies 'with the exception of Huskies' / President: 'Is she not an animation fan or something? Because Huskies was good.'
jokes.setup: The PM is established as a superfan of The Rock
jokes.punchline: The one movie she hasn't seen is 'Huskies' — a fictional (presumably bad) Dwayne Johnson movie. His defense of it — 'Huskies was good' — implies it was not good.
jokes.explanation: Self-deprecating meta-reference to The Rock's filmography with a fake bad movie. The President's defense ('Huskies was good') reads as polite and unconvincing — which makes it funnier. The 'Is she not an animation fan?' question implies the movie was animated, adding an extra absurd layer.

jokes.text: 'Is she not an animation fan or something? Because Huskies was good.'
jokes.setup: Honig hasn't seen 'Huskies.'
jokes.punchline: Dwayne defends 'Huskies' by speculating she has a genre bias against animation — the defensiveness about a presumably bad/obscure movie is funny. He says 'it was good' with no irony.
jokes.explanation: A great character joke. Dwayne's sincere defensiveness about an apparently minor animated film ('it was good') delivered with total conviction is the perfect self-referential celebrity comedy beat. Only works with the real Dwayne Johnson. Near-perfect economy. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: 'I'm honored, Mr. President. Thank you. But no.' / 'Fantastic. Wait...'
jokes.setup: The President has given a rousing appeal — 'America needs you, you are the only man for this job'
jokes.punchline: Dwayne says no. The President says 'Fantastic' reflexively before his brain processes the 'no' — 'Wait...' is the delayed comprehension beat
jokes.explanation: Perfect button for the episode. The structure is flawless: patriotic setup → Dwayne declines → 'Fantastic.' (autopilot positive response) → 'Wait...' (processing). The gap between 'Fantastic' and 'Wait...' is the entire joke, and it lands because the President's automatic affirmation reflex fires before his comprehension does. 'I didn't hear that last bit' as the final line extends it perfectly. This is a 8+ ending gag: economical, perfectly timed, highly quotable.

jokes.text: President's final line: 'Wait, I didn't hear that last bit.'
jokes.setup: He already responded with 'Fantastic. Wait...' to Rocky declining
jokes.punchline: Rather than process the refusal, the President claims not to have heard it — the comedic denial of reality as a coping strategy, or a literal hard-of-hearing joke
jokes.explanation: The episode-closing button. The President choosing selective hearing as his response to rejection is a perfect character beat — it's simultaneously authoritarian (I will simply not acknowledge this), comedically oblivious, and a great final word. Works as a standalone line and as the cap to Joke 57.

tmdb_overview: Liz heads to Chicago to get out of jury duty and on her flight back to New York she is assigned a seat next to Oprah. Liz seizes the opportunity to ask Oprah for advice with some of the problems she's been having. Back in New York, the feud continues between Tracy and Jenna, and Jack's morals are tested by Kenneth after an Olympics snafu.
insight: Observational comedy drives 78-point episode with 1.75 jokes per minute across 46 gags.
